title: MCI Pearls
description: Key MCI facts: definitions, command structure, METHANE, START triage and tags, scene layout, disaster buses and support units, HAZMAT, radiation protection, evacuation and recovery, KED.

pearls.text: MCI (Multi- or Mass Casualty Incident): any incident in which EMS resources — personnel and equipment — are overwhelmed by the number and severity of casualties.
Multi Casualty Incident: the number and/or severity of casualties exceeds the capacity of the initial crew(s), preventing effective management and transport.
Crisis: any event expected to lead to an unstable and dangerous situation. Types: natural, technological, rumors, confrontations, workplace violence, terrorist attack, financial.
Disaster: a sudden accident or natural catastrophe that causes great damage or loss of life. Natural examples: earthquake, flood, typhoon.

Man-made disasters: outbreak, fire, landslide, industrial/construction disaster, multiple RTA (train, plane crash, ship), pollution (environmental), public disturbance (riot, rally), event disaster (stampede).
Impacts of disaster: loss of life · loss of property or livelihood · disruption of lifestyle · disruption of government systems · national economic loss · sociological and psychological effects.
Resilience: the ability of individuals to withstand hazards or to recover from the disruption a disaster causes.
Gold = Strategic (CEO) · Silver = Tactical (Head of Operations / Disaster — EMS Commander) · Bronze = Operational (Incident Commander on scene).
First unit on scene temporarily assumes command: the senior medic becomes Incident Commander and the 2nd medic becomes Triage Officer.
The Incident Commander is the only position staffed at every incident. The IC runs everything from the Incident Command Post.

Operation flow: Emergency → DCAS Main Dispatch → first unit on scene (temporary IC) → METHANE report → Main Dispatch → DCAS Disaster Plan → field support units + private hospitals & EMS companies hotline → treatment & transport → recovery phase.

Sector officers: Triage sorts and tags all victims · Treatment runs the treatment area · Transport tells dispatch which hospital each patient goes to · Staging manages incoming resources · Safety gives the IC a risk assessment and monitors that medics follow safety procedures.
Tactical report sheet: relay METHANE to Main Dispatch, then keep counts by Immediate / Delayed / Minor / Involved / Morgue, log ambulance units (time arrived / departed) and the services requested.
M – Major incident declared · E – Exact location · T – Type of incident · H – Hazards · A – Access · N – Number of casualties · E – Emergency services needed.
Send METHANE to Main Dispatch as soon as the MCI is confirmed — it is what activates the DCAS Disaster Plan.
START = Simple Triage And Rapid Treatment. "Triage" is French for "to sort".
Goal: do the most good for the greatest number of potential survivors. Spend 30–60 seconds per patient and start with the closest victim.
Step 1 — Voice triage: tell everyone who can walk to move to a set point. Walking wounded = GREEN, even with dramatic injuries (e.g., amputated fingers).
Step 2 — Respiration: not breathing → open / reposition the airway. Breathing starts = RED; still not breathing = BLACK. Breathing over 30/min = RED. 30/min or less = check perfusion.
Step 3 — Perfusion: no radial pulse or capillary refill over 2 seconds = RED — control bleeding. Radial pulse present and refill 2 seconds or less = check mental status.
Step 4 — Mental status: follows simple commands = YELLOW. Cannot follow commands = RED.
Memory aid: RPM — "30 · 2 · Can do" (Respiration 30, Perfusion 2 seconds, Mental status: can do).
Only three interventions during triage: open the airway, control severe bleeding, position the patient. No CPR, IV, cooling dressings or splinting.
Secondary triage is done in the treatment area. Physicians arriving on scene work in the treatment area.
Upgrading a patient's priority: tear off the lowest portion of the triage tag.
Patient improves: apply a new tag and keep the old one attached to it.
Contaminated portion: complete it before transport so a contaminated patient is not sent to a hospital that cannot handle the case, and the receiving hospital can prepare.
SLUDGEM on the tag (nerve-agent signs): Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI upset, Emesis, Miosis.
Treatment tarps from the exit/loading side: RED nearest the exit, then YELLOW, then GREEN. BLACK is kept away from the others.
Spacing: 5 m between tarps · 1 m between patients (backboard to backboard).
Areas to set up: collection area, triage area, treatment area (red / yellow / green), loading area, and the command post (Bronze command).
Staging area: holds incoming personnel, equipment and supplies — divided into Medics / Paramedics / Advanced Paramedics.
Bus A: 15 patients · 1 surgical room · treatment, surgical, transport.
Bus B: 25 patients · no surgical room · treatment, transport.
Bus C: 33 patients · 1 surgical room · treatment, surgical, transport.
Isnad 5 — ISUZU (Jebel Ali / Mina): 100–150 patients.
Isnad 4 — ISUZU (Hatta): 100–150 patients.
Isnad 3 — DELTA (Warsan): 80–100 patients.
Isnad 2 — MAN (Warsan): about 400 patients.
HAZMAT: any material or substance — solid, liquid or gas — that poses danger to life, property or the environment if improperly stored, shipped or handled.
Hazardous material types: chemical, biological, radiation, nuclear.
Routes into the body: Inhalation (breathing — the most rapid) · Ingestion (swallowing) · Injection (penetrating the skin) · Absorption (through skin or eyes).
Chemical Protective Suit (CPS): protects against hazardous materials in solid, liquid and gas form.
Approaching: stay 100 m away, ensure scene safety and size up. Observe the wind direction and park uphill / upwind.
Stop at a safe distance and try to identify the material: look for warning signs or placards, company files, or ask the driver of the vehicle.
Know the number of casualties, inform dispatch via METHANE, and request backup and the DCD / HAZMAT team. Once HAZMAT is confirmed, upgrade your PPE.
Paramedic goals: Know (evaluate the hazard if possible) · Notification (inform dispatch, request assistance) · Isolation (set a perimeter, deny entry, evacuate) · Protection (no intentional contact).

On scene: no electronic devices · no eating, drinking or smoking · do not touch the materials · secure the area and let in emergency responders only · guide any casualty to the decon area and minimise contact.
Hot (red) zone: the contaminated area — 100 m.
Warm zone: 200 m — contains the contamination-reduction corridor where decontamination happens.
Cold zone: 300–500 m, upwind and uphill — EMS staging and treatment work here.
Decontamination area: for emergency responders and for casualties, by dry-spray or shower decontamination.
Four kinds of placards: HAZMAT · ADR · U-KISS · NFPA.
HAZMAT placard: hazard class / division plus the international (UN) code, company name and contact number.
ADR placard: for hazardous materials transported by road (started in Europe). Orange plate: top = hazard code (e.g., 33), bottom = UN number (e.g., 1203).
U-KISS placard: for storage of hazardous materials (introduced in the UK) — shows management when exposed, proper PPE, and evacuation when at risk.
NFPA 704 "fire diamond": Blue = health · Red = fire · Yellow = instability · White = specific hazard. Ratings run 0 (normal / will not burn / stable) to 4 (deadly / below 73°F / may detonate).
NFPA white section: ACID · ALK (alkali) · COR (corrosive) · OX (oxidizer) · radiation symbol · W with a line through it (use no water).
Time: minimise time in the hazardous environment — also key when assessing contamination of civilians who self-evacuated from the hot zone.
Distance: radiation hazard drops sharply with distance from the source — evacuate and set an appropriate hot zone immediately.
Shielding: solid objects may shield from the source depending on the radiation type — a secondary measure after time and distance.
Evacuation: the immediate, urgent movement of people away from a threat or actual hazard.
Evacuation sequence: detection → decision → alarm → reaction → movement to an area of refuge or assembly station → transportation.
Recovery: returning an organization to normal after a disaster — Relief, Rehabilitation, Restoration.

Prepare: universal precautions · explain the procedure and tell the patient not to move · manual C-spine in neutral · check circulation, motor and sensation (CMS) in all extremities · apply the C-collar.

Position: tilt the patient forward as a unit and examine the back · slide the KED behind, smooth side toward the patient · drop the leg straps down and to the side · pull the device up snug under the armpits.
Strap order: Middle → Bottom → Leg straps (each looped around the same-side leg) → pad behind the head as needed → Head & chin → Thoracic last (push/pull while the patient breathes out).

Finish: hands together (tie thumbs/wrists) · recheck CMS in all extremities · turn patient and device as a unit onto the backboard · loosen the leg straps so the legs extend flat · secure to the backboard.

METHANE report.alt: METHANE: Major incident, Exact location, Type of incident, Hazards, Access, Number of casualties, Emergency services.

START triage.alt: START adult triage flowchart. Able to walk: Minor, then secondary triage. Not breathing: position the airway; breathing starts: Immediate; still apneic: Expectant. Respiratory rate over 30: Immediate. Absent radial pulse or capillary refill over 2 seconds: Immediate. Cannot follow simple commands: Immediate. Otherwise: Delayed.

HAZMAT placards.alt: The four placard types. HAZMAT placard: hazard class and UN number, for example UN 1203 class 3. ADR orange plate: hazard code 33 over UN number 1203. U-KISS placard: hazard, management, PPE and evacuation. NFPA 704 fire diamond: blue health, red fire, yellow instability, white specific hazard, each rated 0 to 4.
